4.final: alameda drain the mrgcd has authorized project funds for engineering and planning services to develop a comprehensive land management and multi use corridor plan for the alameda drain from i 40 upstream to the sandia pueblo boundary the intent is to work towards a three way funding agreement between the mrgcd bernalillo county and city of albuquerque the consolidated engineering and planning effort would assess infrastructure improvements and alternative maintenance techniques to allow for restoration of riparian habitat ditch bank grasses and native shrub and tree communities to transform the drain from a weed choked elm tree growing maintenance intensive blight on the valley to a community asset to be enjoyed by mrgcd constituents infrastructure improvements would b proposed bikeway and trail facilities include assessment of uniform access control crossing structure upgrades management of storm water inflows and evaluation of storm water quality best management practices for storm water flows in the drain multi use components would include assessment and locations of planned trails park nodes community gardens and other public amenities the mrgcd funding would be contingent on matching funds from bernalillo county and the city of albuquerque both agencies have interest in this project to support their nepa permitting and implementation of trails $1m currently funded tree canopy restoration future storm drain connections and other elements as determined through a community planning process open space projects the open space division s current focus for future soft surface trails is in areas of the east mountains and sandoval county properties including the john a milne gutierrez canyon open space and the golden open space the goal is to construct approximately 10 miles of new trail in the golden property and 7 miles for the john a milne gutierrez canyon open space because these trails are built largely with volunteer labor it is expected that these trail networks will be completed within the next five years additionally the osd has been analyzing user created trails in the sandia foothills open space to see which ones can be converted into official trails the process of determining which trails can become official trails entails looking at whether the trail adds to the overall circulation of the trail system or if it is a redundant trail the process also involves looking at the grades and the amount of erosion on the user trails and weighing the potential for adding erosional control features such as drain dips and rerouting severely eroded sections drain dips are defined in the osd trails design guidelines if the trail can be converted to a sustainable condition minimum maintenance required or maintainable condition substantive_chapter_findings.finding: Final adds explicit four-year plan updates and annual map updates, a fuller glossary including buffered/protected lanes and cycle tracks, open-space and user definitions, and safety-in-numbers discussion. This is substantive revision of the introduction, not merely repagination.

Goals and Policies becomes Goals and Principles. Goal 1 changes from improving cyclist/pedestrian safety to improving/enhancing cycling/pedestrian opportunities. Final adds pilot testing of practices, an explicit 5-percent walking/biking trip target to the use principle, performance measures and more open-space/plan relationships. It establishes NACTO as governing in conflicts with AASHTO in developed urban areas, unless project funding stipulates otherwise. The 5-percent target also occurs in the draft federal-policy discussion; it is not wholly new to the family.

The final expands open-space trail inventory and ADA context, specifying just over 100 miles managed by Open Space and the limited scope of the 1996 ADA survey. It revises user needs, collision analysis and maintenance reporting/YARDI discussion. It removes the draft assertion that overpasses are crucial at Paseo del Norte/Coors and east I-40/Rio Grande. Draft opportunities-and-constraints PDF45 is a TIFF placeholder, whereas final provides the mapped material.

Draft PDF60 contains a substantial Arterial Shared Roadway Measures discussion and treatment list absent from this chapter of the final. The final includes updated construction/gap context at Paseo del Norte, San Pedro, Corrales Main Canal and Bridge Boulevard, expanded project selection/public input, and Alameda Drain context. Current-project tables are largely reordered; critical-link segments are merged/revised (e.g. Coors Central-Saint Joseph 2.92+0.46 becomes3.38 miles; Irving segments0.77+0.63 become1.40). Sage segments and other lengths/endpoints change. Draft PDFs69-72 are four map-caption placeholders; final includes quadrant proposed-network, current-project and critical-link maps. Table9 full-build planning estimate changes from$121,168,000 to$143,207,000, with changed facility quantities and added HAWK signals; unchanged unit prices alone do not make the files duplicates.

cost_table.caution: Narrative and table quantities/totals have internal inconsistencies within each original. Findings identify the specific Table9 rather than silently correcting or harmonizing original statements.

substantive_chapter_findings.finding: Final adds Bicycle Friendly Community five-E context, Open Space environmental education, enforcement recommendations, the September2014 ABQ CiQlovia event and local counters; it adds a substantial bike-share proposal and electric-cycle, water-trail and Smart Trips possibilities. These post-draft additions distinguish programs available for comparison.

Draft PDFs100-103 preserve earlier committee criticisms, complete Tucson/Pima, Minneapolis and Moreno Valley case descriptions, and a City Council/Mayor staffing option. Final PDFs140-142 revises the public-input/combined-committee alternatives, removes the extended peer case studies and Mayor/Council staffing option, and adds separate pedestrian-plan/input discussion. Final adds arroyo/ditch and development-acceptance requirements, IDO/DPM update language, on-street maintenance responsibilities, maintenance maps and a multi-page implementation summary. Implementation matrix: draft PDF124 ID22 proposes five-year updates, final PDF174 ID22 four-year; draft ID27 Complete Streets ordinance becomes LAB recommendations/performance measures and final adds annual ADA transition plans. Final also adds deficient lane-width inventory, top crash locations and 311 work-order closure.

Only the final file integrates the129-page design manual: on-street facilities, trails, intersections, wayfinding, markings and maintenance. The131-page file references a separately delivered Chapter7 in its TOC and text but does not contain it. Neither this131-page file nor the312-page core final physically includes the separately listed A-H appendices; TOC listings are not proof of inclusion.

The final has expanded contents/list-of-figures/acknowledgments and the scanned Council resolution/enactment, followed by a Chapters1-6 index at PDF312. Draft has a2014 cover and no adoption resolution. Final cover is May2015; Council signature page PDF7 records May18,2015 passage; clerk memorandum PDF8 dated June3,2015 certifies the resolution in force without a mayor signature.

comparison_limitations: Normalized word diffs and page-shingle matches are inspection aids: headers, wrapping, reordered tables and scanned pages prevent a raw mismatch count from equaling a substantive change count. All443 pages rendered and inspected in contact sheets; scanned enactment pages and selected dense/changed pages inspected at full resolution. Conclusions use complete chapters and explicit page references, not metadata/page totals alone.
